abstract: This study used large-scale randomized controlled experiments during the 2020 US presidential election to test how Facebook's and Instagram's machine-learning feed-ranking algorithms affect users' political attitudes and behaviors. Consenting users were randomly assigned to a reverse-chronological feed instead of the default algorithmic feed for roughly three months (September–December 2020). While the chronological feed substantially altered users' on-platform experience—reducing time spent, engagement, and changing the mix of content seen—it produced no detectable changes in downstream political outcomes such as polarization, political knowledge, or offline participation.
key_claims: Social media feed-ranking algorithms strongly shape users' on-platform experiences, including time spent, engagement, and the type and source of content they see.

Despite these large experiential effects, replacing algorithmic ranking with reverse-chronological ordering did not measurably change affective polarization, issue polarization, political knowledge, or offline political participation over a three-month election period.
Algorithmic feeds may not be the direct root cause of individual-level political polarization or knowledge deficits, tempering popular 'filter bubble' and folk theories about algorithmic harms.
Isolating the causal role of algorithmic ranking (as opposed to the broader 'bundle' of social media features) reveals that its measurable political effects on individuals are limited.
methods: Two randomized controlled experiments embedded within Facebook (n = 23,391) and Instagram (n = 21,373), with consenting US adult users recruited via in-feed survey invitations in August 2020.

Treatment group received a reverse-chronological feed from 24 September to 23 December 2020; control group retained the default algorithmic feed (affecting an estimated ~80% of on-platform material; ads unaffected).
Five survey waves combined with on-platform behavioral logs and passive off-platform web-tracking data (fieldwork conducted with NORC at the University of Chicago).

Preregistered design and analysis (OSF) with primary estimand the population average treatment effect (PATE), weighted by predicted ideology, friend count, political pages followed, and days active; unweighted sample average treatment effects (SATE) also reported.

Content classified along dimensions including political content, political news, ideological cross-cutting vs. like-minded vs. moderate/mixed sources, untrustworthy sources, incivility, and slur words; heterogeneity and subgroup analyses conducted.
Study conducted as a collaboration between Meta and external academics, with Meta funding data-collection costs but no prepublication approval rights and academic lead authors holding final control.
findings: The chronological feed sharply reduced time spent: average daily time above US monthly active users fell from +73% to +37% on Facebook and +107% to +84% on Instagram; users also substituted toward TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, and Instagram.
On-platform engagement dropped: Facebook likes fell from 6.7% to 3.1% of exposures; comparable declines occurred for Instagram likes and comments.

Content mix shifted: chronological feeds increased political content and political news, increased untrustworthy-source content (Facebook 2.6%→4.4%; Instagram 1.3%→1.6%), and decreased uncivil content on Facebook (3.2%→1.8%) and slur-word content.

On Facebook, chronological feeds reduced both like-minded (53.7%→48.1%) and cross-cutting (20.7%→18.7%) sources while increasing moderate/mixed-audience sources (22.6%→30.9%); friend-sourced content dropped ~24 percentage points.
No significant treatment effects on affective or issue polarization, election knowledge, news knowledge, self-reported participation, or self-reported turnout on either platform.
On-platform political engagement declined significantly (Facebook −0.117 SD; Instagram −0.090 SD), consistent with an overall drop in engagement.

Among secondary outcomes, the only significant effect was that Facebook chronological-feed users clicked more on partisan political news (0.107 SD), attributed to increased exposure to frequently posted partisan news links.
contributions: Provides rare, large-scale experimental evidence isolating the causal effect of proprietary feed-ranking algorithms (rather than the whole social media 'bundle') on political attitudes and behavior.
Demonstrates a striking disconnect between large algorithm-induced changes in user experience and negligible changes in downstream political outcomes, informing debates over algorithmic regulation.
Establishes a well-defined counterfactual (reverse-chronological ranking) matching policy proposals, offering a methodological template for evaluating machine-learning feed systems.
Contributes deidentified data and code via the Social Media Archive (SOMAR) for replication and IRB-approved research.
framing: The paper positions itself within research on social media, algorithms, and democracy, engaging directly with 'filter bubble,' echo-chamber, and polarization theories and public/regulatory concerns about opaque feed-ranking systems. It responds to prior work that treated social media as an undifferentiated bundle by isolating personalized algorithmic ranking as a distinct causal factor, and situates findings within political communication and computational social science debates about the drivers of polarization.
